content: Flavin is a tricyclic heteronuclear organic ring structure derived from the vitamin riboflavin. This flavin moiety is frequently conjugated with an adenosine diphosphate molecule to form flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD). Alternatively, it can exist as flavin mononucleotide (FMN), which is a phosphorylated derivative of riboflavin. In these forms, flavin functions as a prosthetic group in flavoproteins. The flavin group is biochemically significant due to its ability to participate in oxidation-reduction (redox) reactions. It can accept electrons either one at a time in a two-step process or two electrons simultaneously. In its reduced form, FADH2, flavin serves as a cofactor capable of transferring electrons to the electron transport chain, a critical component of cellular respiration. Flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) acts as a prosthetic group that is tightly bound to various enzymes, including ferredoxin-NADP+ reductase, monoamine oxidase, D-amino acid oxidase, glucose oxidase, xanthine oxidase, and acyl-CoA dehydrogenase. FADH and FADH2 are the reduced forms of FAD. Specifically, FADH2 is generated as a prosthetic group in succinate dehydrogenase, an enzyme integral to the citric acid cycle. Additionally, FADH2 is involved in other enzymatic systems, such as E. coli nitroreductase and the old yellow enzyme.
